catalysts.description: Chief-executive transition: an incoming CEO becomes Chairman and CEO effective March 1, 2019, following an interim CEO who served from January 1 to March 1, 2019 [g8].
Full-year 2019 product-sales guidance of $21.3-21.8 billion, explicitly built around anticipated new U.S. and European generic competition [g7].

unresolved_questions: Whether HIV franchise growth (led by the 2018 launch) can keep outpacing the ongoing hepatitis C decline as anticipated 2019 generic competition affects two other products.
Whether the earlier-stage oncology and liver-disease pipeline can diversify revenue beyond the HIV/HCV franchises before further competitive erosion.
How the incoming CEO transition, effective March 1, 2019, affects capital-allocation priorities such as R&D spending, buybacks and business development.

macro_context.item: Management's 2019 guidance and its own forward-looking risk disclosure both flagged anticipated U.S. and European generic competition -- for two non-antiviral products, for continuing tenofovir disoproxil fumarate erosion in Europe, and for two older antiviral HIV products -- as a headwind [g7][g14].
macro_context.business_connection: This is the structural generic-competition backdrop shaping the company's official 2019 product-sales guidance range.

macro_context.item: The hepatitis C franchise's decline was attributed to lower average selling prices and lower sales volume amid increased competition and fewer new patients starting treatment [g4].
macro_context.business_connection: This is the industry-level dynamic behind why the hepatitis C franchise, once the company's largest, continues shrinking even as the HIV franchise grows.

own: HIV product sales grew to $14.6 billion from $13.0 billion behind the 2018 launch, lifting HIV to about 66% of total revenue from about 50% a year earlier -- evidence the newest franchise addition is more than offsetting the hepatitis C decline [g3][g20].

The company generated $8.4 billion of operating cash flow and held $31.5 billion of combined cash and investments at year-end 2018, even after paying $3.0 billion of dividends, repurchasing $2.9 billion of stock and repaying $6.3 billion of debt during the year [g6].

Two-year follow-up data on the approved cell-therapy product (39% of patients in an ongoing response) and an early signal in a related leukemia study (69% complete remission) suggest the CAR-T franchise, still only $264 million of FY2018 sales, has room to expand within its approved and pipeline indications [g11][g10].
flat: Management's own full-year 2019 product-sales guidance of $21.3-21.8 billion is roughly flat to down versus FY2018's $21.7 billion, explicitly built around anticipated new U.S. and European generic competition [g7].

Total revenue fell to $22.1 billion from $26.1 billion and GAAP operating margin fell to 37.1% from 54.1%, so even with the HIV offset, overall scale and profitability both declined for the year [g2][g16].
short: Hepatitis C product sales fell to $3.7 billion from $9.1 billion in a single year -- a franchise that once anchored the company's growth -- and management's own risk disclosure separately flagged expected erosion from generic versions of two older HIV products [g4][g14].

R&D expense growth included an $820 million impairment on an early-stage, in-licensed multiple-myeloma program, and full-year results absorbed a Q4 2018 unfavorable $0.99-per-share impairment/tax charge tied to the 2017 cell-therapy acquisition -- signs of integration costs still working through results [g19][g18].

scene.voice: Stay away. Their hepatitis C business fell from $9 billion to under $4 billion in one year, the guidance for this year is flat to down, and they just wrote off an $820 million oncology bet. It's a value trap.

scene.question: Is a shrinking franchise with $31 billion of cash and a growing HIV business a trap, or a business already priced for decline?

ask_friend.q: How fast is the old business shrinking?
ask_friend.a: Hepatitis C product sales fell to $3.7 billion from $9.1 billion in one year, a decline management attributes to fewer patients starting treatment and lower prices [g4]. Total revenue fell to $22.1 billion from $26.1 billion and GAAP operating margin to 37.1% from 54.1% [g2][g16]. Guidance for 2019 product sales is $21.3 to 21.8 billion, roughly flat, and it explicitly assumes US generic competition for two older products [g7][g14].

HIV product sales rose to $14.6 billion from $13.0 billion on the 2018 launch of a new single-tablet regimen, now about 66% of revenue [g3][g20]. A 96-week Phase 3 study reported that regimen non-inferior to a competitor [g13]. The cell-therapy business bought in 2017 generated $264 million [g5], with two-year follow-up data and an early study in a second leukaemia population [g10][g11]. A new chief executive starts on 1 March [g8]. Three early immuno-oncology collaborations were signed in the quarter [g9].

ask_friend.q: Is it cheap enough to be a trap?
ask_friend.a: The last close is $70.05, down 14% over twelve months and 15% below the 12-month high. Market capitalisation is about $91 billion; with $31.5 billion of cash and investments against debt, net cash is about $4 billion and enterprise value about $86 billion, roughly 3.3 times 2017 revenue [g6]. Operating cash flow was $8.4 billion after $3.0 billion of dividends and $2.9 billion of buybacks. The year also absorbed an $820 million write-off of an early oncology programme [g19].

claims.text: the company reported fourth-quarter 2018 product sales of $5.7 billion, full-year 2018 product sales of $21.7 billion, full-year GAAP diluted EPS of $4.17 and full-year non-GAAP diluted EPS of $6.67 [g1].
Full-year 2018 total revenues were $22.1 billion, down from $26.1 billion in 2017 [g2].

Full-year 2018 HIV product sales grew to $14.6 billion from $13.0 billion in 2017, driven by the 2018 launch of its newest single-tablet HIV regimen and continued uptake of several other newer HIV combination products [g3].

Full-year 2018 hepatitis C (HCV) product sales fell to $3.7 billion from $9.1 billion in 2017, a decline management attributed to lower average selling prices and lower sales volume for its flagship HCV regimens amid increased competition and fewer new patients starting treatment [g4].
The company's CAR-T cell-therapy oncology product, launched in the United States in October 2017, generated $264 million in sales for full-year 2018, including $81 million in the fourth quarter [g5].

The company held $31.5 billion of cash, cash equivalents and marketable debt securities at December 31, 2018, down from $36.7 billion a year earlier; during 2018 it generated $8.4 billion of operating cash flow, repaid $6.3 billion of debt, paid $3.0 billion in cash dividends and spent $2.9 billion on stock repurchases [g6].

Management's full-year 2019 product-sales guidance of $21.3-21.8 billion explicitly reflects the anticipated U.S. entry of generic competition for two of its non-antiviral products and the full-year European impact of generic tenofovir disoproxil fumarate products [g7].
The company announced a chief-executive transition: an incoming CEO was named Chairman and CEO effective March 1, 2019, with an interim CEO serving from January 1 to March 1, 2019 [g8].

During the fourth quarter the company announced three new early-stage research collaborations aimed at immuno-oncology and fibrotic-disease drug discovery with three separate biotechnology partners [g9].

In an updated Phase 1/2 study (ZUMA-3) of an investigational CD19-targeted CAR T-cell therapy in adults with relapsed or refractory acute lymphoblastic leukemia, 69% of evaluable patients achieved complete tumor remission after a single infusion, with undetectable minimal residual disease in 100% of those complete responders, at a median follow-up of 15.1 months [g10].

Two-year follow-up data from the pivotal trial of the company's approved CAR-T product in refractory large B-cell lymphoma showed 39% of patients in an ongoing response at a median follow-up of 27.1 months after a single infusion [g11].

An investigational oral compound (an FXR agonist) showed significant improvements in liver biochemistry and cholestasis markers in an early-stage study of patients with primary sclerosing cholangitis, a liver disease [g12].

A 96-week Phase 3 randomized, double-blinded study found the company's newest single-tablet HIV regimen statistically non-inferior to a comparator three-drug HIV regimen in treatment-naive adults [g13].
The company's own forward-looking risk disclosure named expected market-share and price erosion from generic versions of two of its older antiviral products as a risk to future results [g14].
Full-year 2018 GAAP product gross margin was 77.6%, down from 83.0% in 2017; fourth-quarter 2018 product gross margin was 72.4%, down from 78.5% a year earlier [g15].
Full-year 2018 GAAP operating margin was 37.1%, down from 54.1% in 2017 [g16].

Total assets were $63.7 billion and stockholders' equity was $21.5 billion at December 31, 2018 (versus $70.3 billion and $20.5 billion a year earlier); 1,282 million common shares were issued and outstanding at December 31, 2018 [g17].

Fourth-quarter 2018 net income was essentially breakeven ($3 million) versus a $3.9 billion net loss in the fourth quarter of 2017; the 2018 quarter's per-share results included a $0.99 per diluted share unfavorable impact from an impairment and non-cash tax charge tied to intangible assets acquired in the company's 2017 purchase of a cell-therapy company [g18].

Full-year R&D expense growth was driven in part by an $820 million impairment charge on an early-stage, in-licensed multiple-myeloma cell-therapy program, alongside higher up-front collaboration spending and continued integration investment following the 2017 cell-therapy acquisition [g19].

HIV product sales represented about 66% of total 2018 revenue, up from about 50% of total 2017 revenue, as the largest franchise's growth (helped by the 2018 launch) outweighed the shrinking hepatitis C business.
